title: Since I held your feet
hookLine: since I grasped Your feet I look to no one else (Chaupai, savaiya)

lines: A TODDLER HOLDING A PARENT'S LEG.
LET GO, AND THE CROWD IS TERRIFYING.
WHAT CHANGED WAS THE HOLDING ON.
cards: A busy market, or a big family wedding, and a toddler in the middle of it, holding a parent's leg. Fine, as long as they're holding on. They'll peer out at the noise and the strangers, even smile.
The second they let go and lose sight of that leg, the whole world becomes terrifying. The crowd didn't change. What changed was whether they were holding on.
Near the end of Chaupai, the meter shifts into a savaiya, a longer, rolling line, and the poet describes exactly that.

teach.b: In paraphrase, the verse begins: since I grasped your feet, I have not brought anyone else under my eye. Feet again. Near the start of the prayer, the mind rested at the Lord's feet.
Here the poet has grabbed hold.

In South Asian custom, touching someone's feet is what you do before a person you deeply honor, a grandparent, a teacher. To grasp them and not let go is the gesture of someone who has decided where they belong.

In paraphrase: Ram and Rahim, the Puranas and the Qur'an speak of many views, and I have not taken one as my own; the Smritis, Shastras and Vedas tell of many mysteries, and I know none of them; by your grace, O sword-bearer, I have not said this, it is all your own telling.
Two things are worth hearing carefully. First, readers take this in more than one way.
Sikh teachers often hear it as single-pointed trust rather than a ruling on other scriptures, and point out that the Guru Granth Sahib itself holds the words of Hindu and Muslim saints.
On that reading, it's about where the poet's own eyes rest: holding the feet, you stop shopping among opinions.

teach.h: I HAVE NOT SAID THIS; IT'S ALL YOU.
teach.b: Second, the last line: I have not said this; it's all you. The Tenth Guru, poet, leader, founder of the Khalsa, signs the verse by saying it isn't his. One good word for that posture is trust.
Not a list of things believed. A grip.
Since I held your feet, the crowd has stopped being frightening.

how: Many Sikhs recite this savaiya as part of Chaupai Sahib, and it is also included in the evening Rehras; touching the feet of elders and teachers is a common sign of deep respect in Punjabi culture.

games.q: you're surrounded by voices, books and opinions, each telling you something different. what does the poet of this savaiya do?
o: argue with each one until he wins.
hold the Lord's feet and look to no one else.
try to follow every opinion at once.
games.why: since I grasped your feet, I have brought no one else under my eye. he holds on, and says the words were never his.

practice: Notice how many things you're half-holding right now: plans, worries, opinions, backup plans for the backup plans.

You don't have to drop them; just choose one thing to trust today, fully, the way a child holds a leg in a crowd, whether God, if you pray, a person who has never let you down, or the fact that you've come through hard days before.
Hold it firmly in your mind, and if you pray, say Waheguru as you do.

wordCard.voice: Charan, feet. Chaupai's savaiya: since I grasped your feet, I look to no one else, and what I've said was never mine.
